fetched_contents.text: Postpartum Depression (PPD): Causes, Symptoms & Treatment What Is Postpartum Depression? Postpartum depression (PPD) is a type of depression that typically happens after childbirth. If you feel extreme sadness or loneliness, have severe mood swings or anxiety, or lose interest in things you normally enjoy, you may have postpartum depression. You can develop it within the first few weeks of your child’s birth or gradually — even up to one year later. But it can also start during pregnancy. Most commonly, it occurs around six weeks postpartum. Postpartum depression doesn’t just affect the mother. It can affect surrogates and adoptive parents, too. People experience hormonal, physical, emotional, financial and social changes after having a baby. These changes can make life feel difficult and you may begin to doubt yourself. If you have postpartum depression, know that you’re not alone, it’s not your fault and that help is available. Some people never seek treatment out of fear or embarrassment. But your healthcare provider is always a safe space to share your symptoms and feelings. They can help you figure out if you need treatment and what treatment will work best for you. Stages and severity of postpartum depression There are three types of postpartum mood disorders — baby blues, postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis. The main difference between them is their severity (or intensity) and how long they last. Postpartum blues or baby blues Most new moms experience postpartum “baby blues,” and this is considered a normal experience. The baby blues affect up to 3 in 4 people after delivery. If you’re experiencing the baby blues, you may cry for no apparent reason or feel anxious a few times a day. Baby blues typically begin within a few days of delivery, but the symptoms tend to subside within a week or two on their own. If symptoms continue beyond your second week postpartum, contact a healthcare provider. Postpartum depression Postpartum depression is more intense and more severe than the baby blues. It can start within one week of delivery and last several months. Symptoms of postpartum depression interfere with your day. Your days tend to feel mostly bad instead of mostly good. You may experience alternating highs and lows, frequent crying, irritability and fatigue. You may also feel that you can’t care for your baby or for yourself. Up to 1 in 7 will develop postpartum depression. Postpartum psychosis Postpartum psychosis is an extremely severe form of postpartum depression that requires emergency medical attention. This condition is rare, affecting 1 in 1,000 people after delivery. The symptoms generally come on quickly and intensely, lasting for many weeks or many months. Symptoms include severe agitation, confusion, feelings of hopelessness, delusions or hallucinations, rapid speech and mania. A note from Cleveland Clinic Postpartum depression can happen to anyone. Having a new baby to care for — while also caring for yourself and other loved ones — can be overwhelming, to say the least. The biological, physical and social factors that cause postpartum depression are beyond your control. It’s not your fault, and you did nothing to cause it. It doesn’t make you a bad parent, and you’re not the first person to feel the way you feel. Everyone has good days and bad days. But if you feel like you have more bad days than good days, it’s time to reach out to your healthcare provider for help. They can figure out the best way to manage your symptoms. Counseling, medication and joining a support group are good ways to help you cope with PPD and get you feeling better. Experts You Can Trust Medically Reviewed.Last updated on 03/26/2026. fetched_contents.text: Baby Blues vs. Postpartum Depression Baby Blues It’s very common for women to have times of highs and lows or to feel “blue” after having a baby. These feelings usually start 2-3 days after birth and can come and go. New mothers may experience feelings of worry, unhappiness, and fatigue. These feelings typically get better within a few weeks. If these feelings last for more than a few weeks or you become concerned about yourself or a new mom, you (or she) could be experiencing postpartum depression. Contact your healthcare provider or call the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline. The National Maternal Mental Health Hotline is a free, confidential service that provides support for pregnant and postpartum people. The hotline is available 24/7 by calling or texting 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262). Symptoms Moms with baby blues can experience: * Weepiness or crying for no apparent reason * Impatience * Irritability * Restlessness * Anxiety * Fatigue * Insomnia (even when the baby is sleeping) * Sadness * Mood changes * Poor concentration How often do women experience the “baby blues?” Approximately 70-80% of all new mothers experience some negative feelings or mood swings after the birth of their child. Researchers believe that depression is one of the most common problems women experience during and after pregnancy. > We now know that women may also experience anxiety around the time of pregnancy, beyond just being nervous about having a baby. Anxiety during and after pregnancy is as common as depression and may even happen at the same time as depression. No matter what you call them, depression and anxiety that happen during pregnancy or after birth are real medical conditions, and they affect many women. How to help Some things moms can do to help relieve baby blues include: * Talk with someone you trust about how you are feeling. * Connect with other moms in your community or online * Postpartum Support International (PSI) can connect you to a South Dakota support coordinator and support groups that meet regularly * The PSI-SD Facebook page is another way to find local online support groups * Postpartum Progress® offers a private online community so you can connect with other moms no matter where you live * WIC breastfeeding peer counselors can be a great first step in building a support network * Maintain a well-balanced diet * Having a new baby may limit the time you have to prepare healthy meals. Too many simple carbohydrates can make mood swings more pronounced. * Make time for yourself – do something you enjoy * Take a walk, take a bath, read, journal, draw, watch a movie, meditate, or find a yoga class. Take a bit of time each day to do something you enjoy. * Be with other adults and make time to be with your partner * Seek out other adults who can provide comfort and company. Set aside regular time for you and your partner, or for you and a friend, to be together. * Be realistic * Don’t expect perfection in the first few weeks. Give yourself time to heal from birth, and for feeding and sleeping routines to settle in. * Rest when the baby rests * Sleep is just as important for you as it is for baby * Ask for help * Whether it’s caring for baby, preparing meals, helping with other children, doing household chores, or getting into a routine, don’t be afraid to ask friends and family to support you so you can focus on the joy of having a new baby and not just the pressure of juggling it all. It interferes with mom’s ability to care for herself and her family. It can occur up to a year after birth. Mothers with postpartum depression experience feelings of extreme sadness, anxiety, and exhaustion that may require treatment. If you are concerned about yourself or a new mom who could be experiencing postpartum depression, contact your healthcare provider or call the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline. The National Maternal Mental Health Hotline is a free, confidential service that provides support for pregnant and postpartum people. The hotline is available 24/7 by calling or texting 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262). Symptoms Moms with postpartum depression: 1. Can be extremely sad or angry without warning 2. Seem foggy or have trouble completing tasks 3. Appear “robotic,” like they are just going through the motions 4. Be very anxious around the baby and their other children 5. Feel guilty and like they are failing at motherhood 6. Have little interest in things they used to enjoy 7. Have scary, upsetting thoughts that don’t go away or thoughts of hurting self or baby 8. Feel intense symptoms of sadness, anxiety, and hopelessness 9. Lose interest in activities or withdraw from friends and family. How common is postpartum depression? On average, 13% of women have symptoms of depression after the birth of a baby. In South Dakota, that average is slightly higher and is more common among American Indian mothers, younger mothers, mothers with less education, lower household income, and unmarried mothers (PRAMS 2018). fetched_contents.text: Postpartum Psychosis: What It Is, Symptoms & Treatment How is postpartum psychosis treated, and is there a cure? Postpartum psychosis is treatable, and a few different approaches may work. Unfortunately, the rarity of this condition means there's limited available research on how to treat it. Some methods are in widespread use, but more research is necessary for experts to understand how best to treat this condition. Because PPP is a mental health emergency, people with this condition need inpatient mental healthcare. This kind of care means trained medical professionals are with them at all times to make sure they’re safe and as comfortable as possible. Involuntary hospitalization Because PPP disrupts a person’s sense of reality, many people who have it are completely unaware that they have a mental health or medical issue. Further complicating this is the fact that delusions and hallucinations may actually make them afraid to seek help. For those reasons, inpatient mental healthcare for PPP is almost always involuntary. That means the person with PPP is rarely the one who chooses to receive care. Instead, family members, friends or other loved ones must decide to have their loved one hospitalized. This is only an option when there’s reason to believe a person could be a danger to themselves or others. Treatment methods The possible treatment methods include: * Medications. * Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Medications Many different medication types can help PPP. The types include: * Antipsychotic medications. * Mood stabilizers. * Antiseizure drugs. * Lithium. Electroconvulsive therapy Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a safe and highly effective method for treating conditions that involve psychosis. This treatment uses a mild electrical current, passed through your brain, to induce a mild seizure. The effects of that seizure cause changes in brain activity that reduce or resolve the effects of PPP. ECT often has a negative reputation because of frightening portrayals in books, TV shows and movies. But ECT happens under general anesthesia, so the person receiving it is asleep and won’t feel any pain or discomfort during the procedure. Once the person is asleep, healthcare providers will place electrodes on the person’s head and pass an electrical current through their scalp and skull and into a specific part of their brain. These seizures usually last less than two minutes, and a provider can use an injectable medication to stop a longer seizure. Most people wake up within 15 minutes after an ECT procedure and can be up and walking around after half an hour. Complications/side effects of the treatments The possible complications and side effects depend on many factors, especially the treatments you receive and the symptoms you have. Because of this, your healthcare provider is the best person to tell you the most likely risks, complications or side effects that you can or should expect. How do I take care of myself or manage symptoms? Because PPP disrupts your ability to tell what’s real and what isn’t, most people aren’t aware that they have a medical issue. That means this isn’t a condition you can take care of or manage on your own. It’s also very rare for people with PPP to recognize the symptoms, even early on. In almost all cases, others close to the person with PPP will notice the symptoms and act to seek care. What you can do before becoming pregnant or giving birth If you have a history of PPP or have conditions like bipolar disorder or schizophrenia (or have a family history of these conditions), it’s important to talk to your healthcare provider about what you can do to plan ahead in case you develop PPP. You also should have a conversation with those closest to you, such as a partner, family member, close friends, etc. These discussions give you a chance to make them aware of your situation and to understand what you want in case you’re unable to make decisions or act for the safety of yourself or your newborn. How soon after treatment will I feel better, and how long does it take to recover from treatment? The recovery timeline for PPP depends on many factors, including the specific treatment or medication. Your healthcare provider is the best person to tell you what’s most likely to happen in your case, and can provide information and guidance that’s relevant to you.

Distinguish normal postpartum adjustment from possible mental health concern

The evidence clearly indicates that early postpartum adjustment is common and often includes temporary emotional ups and downs, while more persistent symptoms point toward a possible mental health condition. In the early postpartum period, many new mothers experience “baby blues,” which are described as a normal reaction after childbirth. These feelings usually start 2–3 days after birth and can come and go; they often include worry, unhappiness, fatigue, irritability, restlessness, anxiety, insomnia, sadness, mood changes, and poor concentration. The South Dakota Department of Health report says these feelings typically get better within a few weeks [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic likewise notes that baby blues are very common, affecting up to 3 in 4 people after delivery, and that symptoms usually subside within a week or two on their own [N1-F1]. If symptoms continue beyond the second week postpartum, the Cleveland Clinic recommends contacting a healthcare provider [N1-F1]. 

For normal adjustment, the duration is generally short and self-limiting. The baby blues are not considered a medical disorder, but the postpartum period can also include more intense emotional strain as the body and life adjust to parenthood [N1-F1]. However, when symptoms are more severe or persistent, the distinction becomes clearer. Postpartum depression is more intense and more severe than the baby blues, can start within one week of delivery and last several months, and interferes with daily functioning. The Cleveland Clinic states that postpartum depression symptoms include extreme sadness or loneliness, severe mood swings or anxiety, and loss of interest in things normally enjoyed, and that it can occur up to one year after birth [N1-F1]. The South Dakota Department of Health similarly emphasizes that postpartum depression is more serious than baby blues and can start within the first few weeks after birth, interfering with a mother’s ability to care for herself and her family [N2-F2]. 

The evidence also distinguishes sadness from depression, anxiety, and psychosis. Sadness alone is not necessarily abnormal, especially in the early postpartum period. However, the line becomes more serious when sadness becomes persistent, severe, or accompanied by other symptoms. The Cleveland Clinic explains that postpartum depression can include alternating highs and lows, frequent crying, irritability, fatigue, and the feeling that one cannot care for the baby or oneself [N1-F1]. The South Dakota Department of Health adds that mothers with postpartum depression may experience extreme sadness or anger without warning, appear foggy or have trouble completing tasks, seem “robotic,” be very anxious around the baby and other children, feel guilty or like they are failing at motherhood, have little interest in things they used to enjoy, and may have scary, upsetting thoughts that do not go away or thoughts of hurting self or baby [N2-F2]. These are red flags that go beyond normal adjustment and suggest a more serious condition.

The evidence on psychosis is particularly important because it represents the most immediate concern. Postpartum psychosis is described as a mental health emergency and is rare but very dangerous. The Cleveland Clinic states that it affects 1 in 1,000 people after delivery, with symptoms including severe agitation, confusion, feelings of hopelessness, delusions or hallucinations, rapid speech, and mania [N1-F1]. The South Dakota Department of Health similarly describes postpartum psychosis as a serious mental illness that should be treated as a medical emergency, with symptoms that disrupt a person’s sense of reality [N2-F2]. The key distinction here is that psychosis is not merely a more intense version of sadness; it involves a break with reality, delusions, hallucinations, and a risk to self or others that warrants urgent intervention [N4-F3].

In short, the early postpartum period can include normal sadness and emotional fluctuation, but persistent sadness, severe mood swings, anxiety, exhaustion, or thoughts of self-harm or harm to the baby are signs that a more serious condition may be present. The evidence supports treating baby blues as temporary and common, while postpartum depression and psychosis are distinct conditions that require different levels of urgency and care [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Provide actionable advice on what the patient should do next

The evidence strongly supports an immediate but thoughtful next step: seek professional help as soon as symptoms are concerning, but also take practical self-care steps while waiting. The Cleveland Clinic says that if symptoms continue beyond the second week postpartum, a healthcare provider should be contacted [N1-F1]. The South Dakota Department of Health similarly advises that if feelings last for more than a few weeks or if someone becomes concerned about themselves or a new mom, they should contact a healthcare provider or the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline [N2-F2]. The ACOG resource also frames postpartum depression as a health condition that can be treated with medication and therapy, reinforcing that professional evaluation is appropriate when symptoms persist [N6-F4]. 

The evidence also makes it clear that some situations require immediate help. Postpartum psychosis is a mental health emergency, and the Cleveland Clinic explicitly states that it requires inpatient mental healthcare because it disrupts a person’s sense of reality and can be dangerous [N4-F3]. If a person has symptoms such as severe agitation, confusion, delusions, hallucinations, rapid speech, or thoughts of hurting self or baby, the evidence supports treating this as an urgent situation [N1-F1][N4-F3]. In such cases, the patient should not delay; they should contact emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department. The South Dakota Department of Health also emphasizes that if a person is concerned about someone who may be experiencing postpartum depression, they should contact a healthcare provider as soon as possible [N2-F2].

For less urgent concerns, the evidence suggests a step-by-step approach. First, the patient should consider whether the symptoms are new or worsening, and whether they are interfering with daily life. The Cleveland Clinic advises that postpartum depression can start within one week of delivery and last several months, and that it can occur up to one year after birth [N1-F1]. The South Dakota Department of Health adds that postpartum depression can last for months or years without treatment [N2-F2]. This means that if sadness, anxiety, or exhaustion are persistent and not improving, professional help should be sought sooner rather than later [N2-F2]. The evidence also supports asking a doctor or therapist specific questions to clarify the concern. The patient should ask whether the symptoms fit a normal adjustment, whether they are consistent with baby blues, postpartum depression, or psychosis, and what treatment options are available [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-F4]. They should also ask about whether the symptoms are dangerous, whether hospitalization might be needed, and whether a mental health professional can help [N4-F3][N6-F4].

Practical self-care steps are also supported by the evidence. The South Dakota Department of Health recommends talking with someone you trust, connecting with other moms in the community or online, maintaining a well-balanced diet, taking time for oneself, resting when the baby rests, asking for help, and being realistic about the demands of new parenthood [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic similarly says that counseling, medication, and joining a support group are good ways to cope with postpartum depression [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic and ACOG both point to psychotherapy, counseling, and therapy as core treatment options [N5-R4][N6-R4]. These self-care steps are especially important while waiting for professional help, but they are not a substitute for medical evaluation. The evidence also notes that many women experience postpartum depression or anxiety, and that it is common and treatable with support [N4-R5]. 

Overall, the actionable advice is straightforward: if the sadness is persistent, severe, or accompanied by anxiety, exhaustion, or thoughts of self-harm or harm to the baby, seek professional help immediately. For less urgent concerns, contact a healthcare provider as soon as possible, and while waiting, take self-care steps such as talking to someone, getting support, resting, eating well, and asking for help from friends or family [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N5-R4][N6-F4].

The evidence identifies several personal, social, and medical factors that increase the risk of postpartum sadness, with sleep, stress, and relationship support playing a central role. Postpartum sadness is not simply a reaction to a new baby; it is shaped by biological, physical, emotional, financial, and social changes after childbirth [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic states that postpartum depression can occur around six weeks postpartum, but can also start during pregnancy and persist up to one year later [N1-F1]. The South Dakota Department of Health adds that postpartum depression is more common among American Indian mothers, younger mothers, mothers with less education, lower household income, and unmarried mothers [N2-F2]. These are important risk indicators that should be considered when assessing the patient’s situation.

Sleep is a major contributor to mood. The South Dakota Department of Health notes that sleep is just as important for the mother as for the baby, and that the patient should rest when the baby rests [N2-F2]. The evidence also implies that sleep deprivation can worsen emotional functioning because many new mothers experience fatigue and insomnia, especially in the early postpartum period [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Poor sleep can intensify sadness and anxiety, making it harder to cope with the demands of parenthood [N2-F2]. 

Stress is another key factor. The evidence repeatedly frames postpartum adjustment as a time of overwhelming change, and the Cleveland Clinic notes that postpartum depression can happen to anyone because of biological, physical, emotional, financial, and social factors [N1-F1]. The South Dakota Department of Health similarly describes anxiety as one of the most common problems women experience during and after pregnancy, and notes that anxiety can happen at the same time as depression [N2-F2]. Stress from caring for a newborn, juggling household responsibilities, and adjusting to a new role can all contribute to emotional strain. The evidence also emphasizes that women should be realistic and not expect perfection in the first few weeks [N2-F2]. This suggests that stress management and realistic expectations are important protective factors.

Relationship support is also a major determinant of mood. The South Dakota Department of Health recommends asking for help from friends, family, and others so the mother can focus on the joy of having a new baby rather than the pressure of juggling everything [N2-F2]. The evidence also supports connecting with other moms in the community or online, joining support groups, and talking with someone you trust [N2-F2]. These social supports can buffer the effects of stress and isolation, which are known risk factors for postpartum mood disorders [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic similarly says that counseling, medication, and joining a support group are good ways to cope with postpartum depression [N1-F1]. 

Family history of mental illness should also be considered, although the evidence provided does not give a complete family-history checklist. Still, the risk literature is clear that perinatal mental health is influenced by genetics, environment, and brain changes [N3-R4]. The evidence on postpartum depression also notes that risk factors include hormonal changes, sleep deprivation, stress, and other physical and social stressors [N3-R4]. The evidence on postpartum psychosis is especially relevant because it states that people with a history of postpartum psychosis, bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia, or those with a family history of these conditions, should talk to their healthcare provider before pregnancy or childbirth [N4-F3]. This implies that a family history of mental illness is a meaningful risk factor that should be discussed with a provider.

In summary, the patient’s risk profile is shaped by a combination of personal, social, and medical factors. Sleep deprivation, stress, and lack of relationship support all appear to increase vulnerability, while family history of mental illness is a relevant but not fully detailed risk factor in the evidence provided [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R4][N4-F3]. The evidence supports treating postpartum sadness as part of a broader adjustment process, but it also indicates that persistent or severe symptoms may reflect a more serious condition that warrants professional evaluation [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence distinguishes between normal adjustment and possible mental health concern. In the early postpartum period, many women experience “baby blues,” which are described as a normal reaction after childbirth. Symptoms can include severe agitation, confusion, feelings of hopelessness, delusions or hallucinations, rapid speech, and mania [N1-F1]. ## What the patient should know about risk factors and contributing factors

The evidence identifies several factors that can make postpartum sadness more likely. Sleep deprivation is a major one: the South Dakota Department of Health notes that sleep is just as important for the mother as for the baby and recommends resting when the baby rests [N2-F2]. Stress is also important; the evidence says postpartum adjustment is shaped by biological, physical, emotional, financial, and social changes, and that stress can contribute to emotional strain [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The Mayo Clinic and ACOG both point to psychotherapy, counseling, and therapy as core treatment options [N5-R4][N6-R4].

## How to frame the concern in a way that a doctor can quickly understand

The evidence says the patient should describe the symptoms clearly and specifically. A good way to frame the concern is:

“I have been feeling very sad since my baby was born. I don’t know if this is normal or if it is something serious. The sadness has been going on for [duration], and I feel [describe symptoms: tired, anxious, hopeless, unable to care for my baby, etc.]. I also want to know if I should see a doctor immediately or if I can wait.”

The patient should also mention whether they have had thoughts of self-harm, harm to the baby, or other alarming symptoms, because these are red flags for psychosis or severe depression [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Including a brief history of sleep, stress, and support can help the provider assess the patient’s risk profile [N2-F2][N3-R4].

## Bottom line

The evidence supports the view that persistent sadness after childbirth should not be ignored. It is common to feel sad after a baby is born, but persistent, severe, or worsening sadness may signal something more serious, such as postpartum depression or postpartum psychosis. The evidence is clear that early help is important, especially when symptoms are severe or when there are signs of psychosis [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

So the patient should:

1. **Seek help as soon as symptoms are concerning.**
2. **Call a healthcare provider or the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline if symptoms last more than a few weeks or if the person becomes concerned about themselves or their baby [N2-F2].**
3. **Go to the nearest emergency department if there are symptoms of psychosis or thoughts of self-harm or harm to the baby [N4-F3].**
4. **Ask specific questions about what the symptoms mean, what treatment options are available, and whether hospitalization may be needed [N1-F1][N6-F4].**
5. **Take practical self-care steps in the meantime, such as resting when the baby rests, asking for help, connecting with others, and staying realistic about the demands of new parenthood [N2-F2][N5-R4].**

The evidence also reassures the patient that help is available, and that postpartum depression and related conditions are treatable [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-F4]. The most important message is: this is not something to feel ashamed about, and it is not your fault.
